title: Holy water at the door
hook: touching water at the church door recalls your baptism

segments.voice: Yesterday, the parish, and a first Mass, or a first in years. Your line was welcome home.

A small basin of water, fixed to the wall or set on a pillar just inside a Catholic church door. People stop at it before they've even looked up at the altar. They dip two fingers in, touch forehead, heart, shoulders, and walk on. Kids stretch on their toes to reach it. Some people flick a drop onto a friend. It takes two seconds, and a visitor could easily miss it. It's water. That's all. And it isn't all.
screen: `A BASIN BY THE DOOR.` → `TWO FINGERS, TWO SECONDS.` → `WATER, AND NOT ONLY WATER.`

segments.voice: The water in that basin has been blessed by a priest, with a prayer asking God to make it a sign of protection and a reminder of baptism. For Catholics, the way into the Church is water. Often it was in infancy: a baby held over a font while a priest poured water three times and said the words from your very first day: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Jesus says in John's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims: "unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Paul adds a picture: baptism is like being buried with Christ and rising with him. So when a Catholic touches the water on the way in, the body is saying: I came in through water once. I'm coming in again. The door of the church echoes the door of baptism. Catholics call holy water a sacramental, which is a different thing from a sacrament. It isn't magic, and it doesn't work by itself. The Church teaches it's a blessed sign that prepares a person to receive grace, through the Church's prayer and the person's own faith. On some Sundays, especially in the Easter season, the priest walks down the aisle and sprinkles the whole congregation with it. Some people laugh when they get a good splash. Some families keep a little holy water at home, by the front door or the bed. And this week's thread: a French girl digging for a spring, and now a basin at a door. Water keeps showing up.
screen: `BLESSED WATER, BY THE DOOR.` · `YOU CAME IN THROUGH WATER.` · `A SACRAMENTAL, NOT MAGIC.` · `SPRINKLED ON THE WHOLE CROWD.` · then, large: `BORN AGAIN OF WATER AND THE HOLY GHOST.`

segments.voice: Go to a sink, or picture one, and let the water run over your fingers; it isn't holy water, just a reminder, the way a photo reminds you of a face. If you're Catholic, or you'd like to, touch your forehead with the wet fingers, or make the sign of the cross. If not, feel the cold, and remember one beginning in your own life.
Aqua benedicta. Latin for blessed water, touched at the church door to remember the water of baptism.
Your line: every door a baptism. A week that ran from Lourdes, through Thérèse, Kolbe and Teresa, to the cloud of witnesses ends here, in the practices. Day ninety-eight, done.

howItsDone: Catholics dip their fingers in holy water and make the sign of the cross on entering and often on leaving a church; many keep holy water at home, and at some Sunday Masses the priest sprinkles the congregation with it.
